A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated proofs and experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original linear-regression simulations and DCLM language-model pretraining experiments in Section 6, with additional simulations in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds LLM saturation-point fitting and warmup-stable-decay experiments in Appendices C.2–C.3.

M1.justification: Appendix K adds a time-varying-step-size extension of shuffled SGD, using polynomial learning-rate schedules where v1 formulates constant-step training. The regression model, loss, reshuffling mechanism and LLM architecture remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate strongly convex synthetic regression, the power-law and logarithmic-power-law solvable cases, and DCLM language modeling. The added learning-rate experiment uses the existing corpus and task; it introduces no new data domain or input scenario.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons remain multi-epoch training versus one-pass training on fresh data. The new WSD experiment retains the one-pass comparator with an adjusted schedule; no additional external comparison method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The saturation criterion changes from E(K,N)=0.8K to 0.75K. Appendix C.3 introduces a distinct WSD protocol: checkpoints after 2, 4, 8 and 16 epochs receive one additional epoch with learning rate decaying from 0.001 to 0.00001. It specifies a corresponding one-pass schedule and estimates losses at other budgets using fitted curves. The original constant-rate settings remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds a robustness test of whether dataset-size-dependent saturation persists under learning-rate decay, directly probing the constant-rate restriction of v1's LLM evidence. Appendices C.2–C.3 also add explicit saturation-point estimation and logarithmic fitting. The original synthetic scaling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports correlation coefficients for the LLM saturation regressions and documents parametric loss-curve estimation. The fixed data-stream seed statement is unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run confidence intervals or significance tests for these experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds K(0.75,N) approximately equal to 0.80 log N + 5.21 with r=0.97, and the WSD fit 2.35 log N + 5.25 with r=0.96, with N measured in billions of tokens. Marked epochs for 0.5B/1B/2B change from 4.0/4.4/4.8 to 4.8/5.2/5.8 under the revised threshold, so these are not same-setting gains. The original scaling curves and synthetic fitted exponents are retained.

T1.justification: New Appendix K introduces polynomial-schedule definitions, bounded-noise and density assumptions, and Theorems K.1–K.2 with supporting derivations comparing one-pass risk and infinite-epoch minimax risk. Existing proofs also receive corrections, such as O(eta squared) becoming O(eta squared times T) in Lemma G.4. However, v2 introduces algebraic inconsistencies: Section 3's expanded SGD update omits the target-dependent term, and Section 4.2 removes expectations from the bias–variance identity.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claim that larger datasets permit more effective repetition remain. The introduction's empirical contribution becomes more specific: v1 emphasizes increasing reuse efficiency with dataset size, whereas v2 claims that the observed saturation epoch scales linearly with log N.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly explains that logarithmic saturation depends on constant learning rates and discusses condition-number-dependent reuse under polynomial decay. v2 removes v1's direct recommendation to allocate approximately log N epochs, explicitly declines to claim a general logarithmic law for LLMs, and adds learning-rate tuning and finite-epoch decay behavior as unresolved limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices C.2–C.3 document EMA smoothing with coefficient 0.9 and three checkpoints, saturation-point selection, curve-fitting formulas, and WSD checkpoint and decay settings. The original pretraining description and Tables 1–2 are retained unchanged as Appendix C.1.

R1.justification: Appendix B substantially revises the literature comparisons, distinguishing gradient-flow, online-SGD and learning-rate-schedule analyses and adding functional-scaling-law work, including Li et al. (2026a,b) and Wang et al. (2026). It also changes v1's description of prior SGD results as upper or matching lower bounds to an assertion that they provide only upper bounds. The central comparisons with Muennighoff et al. and Lin et al. remain.

P1.justification: Much of the main related-work discussion moves into Appendix B, while the LLM results, conclusion and appendix proof guides are substantially rewritten. v2 creates a separate strongly convex proof outline and restructures the LLM appendix into setup, fitting and WSD subsections, materially changing narrative organization and proof navigation.

P2.justification: v1's two-panel LLM Figure 2 moves to the introduction as v2's three-panel Figure 1, with an added saturation-fit panel and revised captions and annotations. v2 adds WSD Figure 3. The synthetic figures remain as renumbered Figures 2 and 4, and the table structures are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The WSD experiment, documented saturation fits and explicit discussion of learning-rate dependence improve the empirical support and qualification of v1's central claim. Appendix K partly addresses the previous constant-rate restriction. These gains are tempered by unresolved finite-epoch decay behavior and newly introduced algebraic errors in Sections 3 and 4.2, limiting the overall improvement despite the substantial additions.
